a1-01.explain: Ask '¿Qué hora es?' (What time is it?). Answer 'Son las + number' for two to twelve: Son las tres. One o'clock is singular: Es la una. Add 'de la mañana', 'de la tarde' or 'de la noche'. Watch out: never 'Son las una' or 'Es las dos'.
examples: Son las tres de la tarde en la Ciudad de México.
It is three in the afternoon in Mexico City.
Son las cuatro. ¡No hay flan!
It is four o'clock. There is no flan!
—¿Qué hora es? —Es la una.
"What time is it?" "It's one o'clock."

a1-01.explain: 'Hay' means 'there is' and 'there are' and never changes: hay un flan, hay dos cucharas. 'No hay' means 'there isn't / there aren't'. Watch out: for where a specific, known thing is, use estar: Hay un flan en la cocina, but El flan está en la cocina.
examples: En la cocina hay un flan grande.
There is a big flan in the kitchen.
Son las cuatro. ¡No hay flan!
It is four o'clock. There is no flan!
En la mesa hay una cuchara y unos lentes.
On the table there is a spoon and a pair of glasses.

a1-01.explain: 'Estar' says where someone is and how they feel right now: El abuelo está en la sala. Xóchitl está contenta. Forms: estoy, estás, está, estamos, están. Watch out: English uses 'to be' for everything, but Spanish uses estar (not ser) for location and temporary states.
examples: — ¿Dónde está el flan? —pregunta Xóchitl.
"Where is the flan?" asks Xóchitl.
Chispa, la perra, está en el piso.
Chispa, the dog, is on the floor.
El abuelo Fermín está en la sala.
Grandpa Fermín is in the living room.
—¿Cómo estás? —Estoy bien, gracias.
"How are you?" "I'm fine, thanks."

a1-02.explain: Use 'ser' for the day (Es viernes), for jobs (Delfina es cocinera), for what someone is like (Don Horacio es serio), and for prices and totals (¿Cuánto es? Son cien). The verb agrees with the amount: es un bife, son cien bifes. Watch out: for jobs, Spanish drops 'un/una': es cocinera, not 'es una cocinera'.
examples: Es viernes en Buenos Aires.
It's Friday in Buenos Aires.
Delfina es cocinera en una parrilla.
Delfina is a cook at a steakhouse.
Su jefe, don Horacio, es serio.
Her boss, Don Horacio, is stern.
A las doce: ¡son cien bifes!
At twelve: that's a hundred steaks!

a1-02.explain: 'Gustar' works like 'to please': the thing you like is the subject. Use 'gusta' for one thing and 'gustan' for plural things. The person goes before: me (to me), te (to you), le (to him/her), nos (to us). Watch out: don't say 'yo gusto' or 'le gusta los errores'.
examples: Don Horacio es serio: no le gustan los errores.
Don Horacio is stern: he doesn't like mistakes.
— ¿Tienen bifes? ¡Nos gustan mucho!
"Do you have steaks? We really like them!"
— Me gusta tu bife.
"I like your steak."

a1-02.explain: When a specific person receives the action (is seen, looked at, called), Spanish puts 'a' before them. This 'a' is not translated. Things don't take it: mira a Delfina, but mira la comanda. Watch out: a + el becomes al: Delfina mira al jefe.
examples: Don Horacio mira a Delfina.
Don Horacio looks at Delfina.
El mozo ve a tres clientes nuevos.
The waiter sees three new customers.
Delfina mira la comanda.
Delfina looks at the order ticket. (no 'a': a ticket is a thing)

a1-03.explain: Use 'ser' for what identifies someone: name, origin, nationality, job (es de Chile, es profesora). Use 'estar' for feelings and states right now (está nerviosa, está contenta). Watch out: English uses 'is' for both. 'Es nerviosa' would mean she is a nervous person by nature, not nervous today.
examples: Se llama Alicia y es de Chile.
Her name is Alicia and she is from Chile.
Está muy nerviosa.
She is very nervous.
La profesora es de México y hoy está contenta.
The teacher is from Mexico and today she is happy.

a1-03.topic: Gustar to say what you like
a1-03.explain: 'Me gusta' = I like, 'te gusta' = you like. Use 'gusta' with one thing or an infinitive (an action): me gusta el fútbol, me gusta dibujar. Use 'gustan' with plural things: me gustan los libros. To agree, say '¡A mí también!' (Me too!). Watch out: never 'me gusto' or 'me gustan dibujar'.
examples: — Alicia, ¿te gusta el fútbol? —pregunta.
"Alicia, do you like soccer?" she asks.
— No, me gusta dibujar —responde Alicia.
"No, I like to draw," answers Alicia.
— ¡A mí también! —dice Cristina.
"Me too!" says Cristina.

a1-03.explain: 'Tener' means 'to have' (tengo, tienes, tiene). Spanish also uses it where English uses 'to be' for some feelings: tener hambre (to be hungry), tener sed (to be thirsty), tener frío (to be cold). Watch out: say 'Tengo hambre', not 'Estoy hambre'. 'Hambre' is a noun, so 'very hungry' is 'mucha hambre'.
examples: Tiene el pelo largo y negro.
She has long black hair.
Cristina tiene un bocadillo de queso.
Cristina has a cheese sandwich.
— ¿Tienes hambre? —pregunta Cristina.
"Are you hungry?" asks Cristina.

a1-04.explain: Color words are adjectives. They go after the noun and agree with it in gender and number: chaqueta roja, zapatos blancos, fresas rojas. After es/son they agree too: Tinto es negro. Colors ending in -e or a consonant change only for number: verde, verdes; azul, azules. Watch out: not 'una roja chaqueta' or 'patas blanco'.
examples: Tinto es negro, con las patas blancas.
Tinto is black, with white paws.
Tiene una chaqueta roja porque hace frío.
He wears a red jacket because it's cold.
En la ventana hay una torta blanca con fresas rojas.
In the window there is a white cake with red strawberries.
— Pelo negro, chaqueta roja, zapatos blancos. Va al parque.
"Black hair, red jacket, white shoes. He's going to the park."

a1-04.explain: 'Querer' (to want) and 'poder' (can, to be able to) are followed directly by an infinitive: quiero encontrar, podemos ir. Both change their stem: quiero, quieres, quiere; puedo, puedes, puede (but podemos). Querer can also take a noun: quiero mi torta. Watch out: no extra word for 'to': 'quiero encontrar', not 'quiero a encontrar'.
examples: — Quiero encontrar mi torta.
"I want to find my cake."
¿Me puede ayudar?
Can you help me?
— Podemos ir al parque —dice Edwin.
"We can go to the park," says Edwin.

a1-04.explain: To make a sentence negative, put 'no' right before the verb: no está, no es, no son. If there is a small pronoun such as 'lo' (it), 'no' goes before the pronoun: no lo tengo. Watch out: Spanish has no helper verb like 'don't/doesn't', so 'it isn't him' is simply 'no es él'.
examples: No está en la ventana. No está en la cocina.
It isn't in the window. It isn't in the kitchen.
— No es él, porque es alto —dice Edwin.
"It isn't him, because he's tall," says Edwin.
— ¡No son zapatos, son patas!
"They aren't shoes, they're paws!"

a1-05.explain: 'Querer' (to want), 'necesitar' (to need) and 'poder' (can) are followed by an infinitive: quiero pedir, podemos esperar. Only the first verb changes for the subject; the second stays in the infinitive. Querer and necesitar can also take a noun: necesitan un minuto. Watch out: querer and poder change their stem (quiero, puedes); necesitar is regular.
examples: Quiero desayunar churros con chocolate.
I want to have churros with chocolate for breakfast.
— Podemos esperar —dice el abuelo.
"We can wait," says Grandpa.
¿Puedes hacer los churros, como antes?
Can you make the churros, like before?
Esos churros necesitan un minuto más.
Those churros need one more minute.

a1-05.explain: 'Voy' is the 'I' form of ir (to go): 'Voy a la caja' = I'm going to the till. 'Vamos' = we go / let's go. 'A' means 'to' before a place, and a + el = al (voy al café). Watch out: 'voy a + place' says where you go, but 'voy a + infinitive' says what you're going to do: voy a pedir.
examples: — Voy a la caja. Quiero pedir yo.
"I'm going to the till. I want to order myself."
— ¡Claro! Voy a la cocina.
"Of course! I'm going to the kitchen."
Abuelo, ¿vamos a la chocolatería?
Grandpa, shall we go to the chocolatería?

a1-05.explain: Ask a price with '¿Cuánto es?' (How much is it?) or '¿Cuánto cuesta…?' (How much does … cost?). Use 'cuesta' for one thing and 'cuestan' for two or more. Give a total with 'Son + number + euros': Son diez euros (but one is singular: Es un euro). Tens: diez, veinte, treinta, cuarenta. Watch out: 'cuánto' (how much) is not 'cuándo' (when).
examples: — Un chocolate con churros cuesta cinco euros —dice, sin mirar el menú.
"A chocolate with churros costs five euros," he says, without looking at the menu.
— Dos chocolates con churros, por favor. ¿Cuánto es?
"Two chocolates with churros, please. How much is it?"
— Son diez euros.
"That's ten euros."

a1-01.q: How do you say 'It is four o'clock' in Spanish?
a1-01.why: Four is plural, so use 'Son las cuatro'. Only one o'clock is singular: 'Es la una'. Time never uses estar.

a1-01.q: Fill in the blank: Son las cuatro. ¡No ___ flan!
a1-01.why: 'No hay' means 'there is no'. It says the flan does not exist there any more. 'Está' tells where a known thing is, and 'es' describes.

a1-01.q: Which question asks where the flan is?
a1-01.why: To ask where a specific thing is, use estar: ¿Dónde está el flan? 'Hay' does not go with 'el', and 'es' is not for location.

a1-01.q: Fill in the blank: Chispa, la perra, ___ en el piso.
a1-01.why: Where a specific person or animal is uses estar: Chispa está en el piso. 'Hay' introduces something new, and 'es' describes what something is like.

a1-01.q: Complete: —¿Qué hora es? —___ la una de la tarde.
a1-01.why: One o'clock is singular: 'Es la una'. From two to twelve, use 'Son las…'.

options: Hay una cuchara en la mesa.
Hay la cuchara en la mesa.
Está una cuchara en la mesa.
Una cuchara hay en la mesa.
a1-01.why: 'Hay' introduces something new and goes with un/una, a number or no article, usually first: Hay una cuchara. For a known thing, say 'La cuchara está en la mesa'.

a1-01.q: Put the words in order: sala / abuelo / está / el / en / la
options: El abuelo está en la sala.
El abuelo en la sala está.
Está el abuelo la en sala.
En el abuelo la sala está.
a1-01.why: The usual order is subject + estar + en + place: El abuelo está en la sala (Grandpa is in the living room).

a1-01.q: How do you say 'Xóchitl is happy' (right now)?
a1-01.why: Feelings right now use estar: está contenta. Ser is not used for how someone feels at the moment.

a1-02.q: Fill in the blank: A las doce, ¡___ cien bifes!
a1-02.why: Totals and prices use ser, and the verb agrees with the amount: cien bifes is plural, so 'son'. English says 'that's a hundred', but Spanish does not say 'es cien bifes'.

a1-02.q: Don Horacio doesn't like mistakes (plural). Which sentence is correct?
a1-02.why: With gustar, the thing liked is the subject. 'Los errores' is plural, so the verb is 'gustan'; 'le' (to him) goes before the verb.

a1-02.q: Which sentence needs the personal 'a' in the blank?
options: Delfina pone ___ nueve bifes en la parrilla.
a1-02.why: Personal 'a' goes before a specific person who receives the action: mira a Delfina. La comanda and los bifes are things, so they take no 'a'.

a1-02.q: Fill in the blank: ___ viernes en Buenos Aires.
a1-02.why: Days of the week use ser: Es viernes (It's Friday). 'Está' is for location or feelings, and 'son' is plural.

a1-02.q: How do you say 'Delfina is a cook'?
a1-02.why: Jobs use ser, and Spanish usually drops 'un/una' before a job: Delfina es cocinera.

a1-02.q: Complete: Me ___ tu bife, pero no me ___ las ensaladas.
a1-02.why: The verb agrees with the thing liked: tu bife (one) → gusta; las ensaladas (plural) → gustan. 'Gusto' would mean 'I please'.

a1-02.q: How do you say 'The waiter sees the boss'?
options: El mozo ve a el jefe.
a1-02.why: The boss is a specific person, so he takes personal 'a', and a + el always joins to 'al': ve al jefe.

a1-02.q: The new customers love steaks. Complete: ¡Nos ___ mucho los bifes!
a1-02.why: With gustar the verb agrees with the thing liked. 'Los bifes' is plural, so 'gustan'; 'nos' shows who likes them (us).

a1-03.q: Which sentence is correct for 'She is from Chile and she is nervous today'?
options: Está de Chile y está nerviosa.
Está de Chile y es nerviosa.
Es de Chile y es nerviosa.
Es de Chile y está nerviosa.
a1-03.why: Origin uses ser (es de Chile). A feeling right now uses estar (está nerviosa). 'Es nerviosa' would mean she is a nervous person by nature.

a1-03.topic: Gustar to say what you like
a1-03.q: Alicia answers about soccer. Which answer means 'I like to draw'?
a1-03.why: 'Me gusta' + infinitive = I like to… / I like …ing. With an action the verb is always singular 'gusta'.
Hunger uses tener: tengo hambre (literally 'I have hunger'). 'Hambre' is a noun, so 'very hungry' is 'mucha hambre'.

a1-03.q: At the end of the story: Ahora Alicia tiene una amiga y ___ contenta.
a1-03.why: Being happy now is a feeling, so it uses estar: está contenta. Ser is for origin and identity: es de Chile, es Alicia.
A feeling today uses estar: está nerviosa. Origin (de Chile, de México) and identity (es Alicia) use ser.

a1-03.topic: Gustar to say what you like
a1-03.q: Alicia says: 'Me gusta dibujar.' Cristina likes it too. What does she say?
a1-03.why: To agree with a gustar sentence, say '¡A mí también!' (literally 'to me too'), because the liker is 'a mí', not 'yo'.

a1-03.q: How do you ask 'Are you hungry?'
a1-03.why: Spanish says 'to have hunger': ¿Tienes hambre? English 'are you…?' tempts learners to use estar or ser here.

a1-03.q: Complete: Alicia ___ el pelo largo y negro.
a1-03.why: Spanish describes hair with tener: tiene el pelo largo (literally 'she has the hair long').

a1-04.q: Tinto's paws are white. Complete: Tinto tiene las patas ___.
a1-04.why: Las patas is feminine plural, so the color is feminine plural too: blancas. The color goes after the noun.

a1-04.q: Which sentence means 'I want to find my cake'?
a1-04.why: Querer is followed directly by the infinitive (encontrar), with no 'a'. The 'I' form has the stem change e → ie: quiero.

a1-04.q: How do you say 'It isn't in the kitchen'?
a1-04.why: 'No' goes right before the verb, and location of a specific thing uses estar: no está en la cocina.

a1-04.q: Edwin says the delivery man is not the boy. Complete: — ___ él, porque es alto.
a1-04.why: 'No' goes right before the verb. Saying who someone is uses ser: No es él (It isn't him).

a1-04.q: Marleny has two green jackets. Complete: Marleny tiene dos chaquetas ___.
a1-04.why: Colors ending in -e have no masculine or feminine form; they only add -s for the plural: verdes. 'Verdas' and 'verdos' do not exist.

a1-04.q: Edwin and Marleny want to go to the park together. Complete: ___ ir al parque. (We can…)
a1-04.why: Poder changes o → ue in puedo, puedes, puede, pueden, but NOT in the 'we' form: podemos.
'No' goes directly before the verb: No son zapatos. There is no helper verb like 'don't'.
In Spanish the color usually goes after the noun and agrees with it: la torta is feminine singular, so 'una torta blanca'.

a1-05.q: Which sentence is correct for 'We can wait'?
a1-05.why: Poder changes its stem to 'pued-' only in some forms (puedo, puedes, puede); nosotros is 'podemos'. The second verb stays in the infinitive, with no 'a'.

a1-05.q: What does '— Voy a la caja —dice Nerea' mean?
options: "I'm going to the till," says Nerea.
"She's going to the till," says Nerea.
a1-05.why: 'Voy' is the 'I' form of ir (to go), and 'a' means 'to' before a place. 'I'm at the till' would be 'Estoy en la caja'.

a1-05.q: Nerea wants to know the price at the till. What does she ask?
a1-05.why: '¿Cuánto es?' means 'How much is it?'. 'Cuándo' means 'when', so '¿Cuándo es?' asks about time, not price.

a1-05.q: Fill in the blank: Un chocolate con churros ___ cinco euros.
a1-05.why: Costar changes o → ue: cuesta. One chocolate is singular, so 'cuesta'; two or more things take 'cuestan'.

a1-05.q: Complete: Yo ___ pedir dos chocolates con churros.
a1-05.why: Querer changes e→ie in the stressed forms: yo quiero, tú quieres. 'Quero' does not exist in Spanish.

a1-05.q: Complete: El abuelo y yo ___ a la chocolatería.
a1-05.why: 'El abuelo y yo' = we (nosotros), so ir becomes 'vamos'. 'Voy' is only for 'yo'.

a1-05.q: Answer the price question for two chocolates: — ___ diez euros.
a1-05.why: A total of two or more uses 'son': Son diez euros. Only one is singular: Es un euro.

a1-05.q: '¡Cuarenta años aquí!' How many years is cuarenta?
a1-05.why: Cuatro = 4, catorce = 14, cuarenta = 40, cuatrocientos = 400. The tens end in -enta: treinta, cuarenta, cincuenta.
